headline: Execution Rocks goes dark by day — bass feeding is a nighttime job now
subhead: Warm water from the Throgs Neck to Matinecock has pushed the stripers nocturnal, but fluke and porgies are covering for them in daylight.
body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shop this week asked me straight out — "Frank, what happened to Exec Rocks? I fished the ebb Tuesday morning, marked bait all over the sounder, and couldn't buy a bass." I told him what I've been telling everybody who'll listen the last ten days: the fish didn't leave, they just clocked out for the day shift.

Kings Point is reading 71.6 degrees right now, and that's warm enough to push stripers into a thermal-avoidance pattern — they're not gone, they're just smart. During daylight they're tucked deep on structure, breathing easier in whatever cooler water they can find, and they don't turn on the feed bag hard until the sun drops and the current gets moving again. I've seen this pattern plenty of Julys going back to the '90s. When the western basin runs a few degrees warmer than the middle Sound — and right now it is, with New London still down around 67.6 — the bass here get nocturnal and structure-locked. Execution Rocks, the rockpile off Matinecock Point, the drop at Stepping Stones — they're all still holding bass. You just need to be fishing them after dark or right at first light, not at 10 a.m. with the sun beating down.

I worked Execution Rocks last Thursday night on the last two hours of the outgoing, anchored up-current of the light and drifting live bunker back on a fish-finder rig, 3 ounces of lead, into the wash. Two fish over 30 inches in about ninety minutes, both came right as the tide bottomed out and the current eased to a crawl. That slower water at the bottom of the tide is when these fish commit — they're not fighting hard current, they're just sliding out of the rocks to grab what's drifting past. If you've got the stomach for a midnight run, that's still the highest-percentage bass play in the western Sound right now.

Daytime, though, is a different game — and a good one. Fluke have been steady on the reefs and humps off Matinecock and out toward Hart Island, holding in 25 to 40 feet on the last of the incoming and first two hours of the outgoing. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom with a slight bounce, have been outproducing bulkier rigs — the water's clear enough right now that these fish want a subtle presentation, not a big splashy teaser strip. Nothing gigantic, but a mixed bag of keepers to 22 inches with enough shorts mixed in to keep the rod bending.

Porgies are around the same structure — Hart Island rockpiles, the reef stretch off Matinecock — but I'll be honest with you, the grade is on the small side this year. Plenty of action, sandworms and clam on a high-low rig will keep you busy, but you're not filling a cooler with dinner-plate porgies like you would out east. We flagged that a week back and it's holding true — fun for a kid's rod, not a fish fry.

Bluefish have been the most reliable action of the week and honestly the most fun. They're not deep, they're not subtle, and they don't care what time it is — I've had them busting bait off the Throgs Neck at noon and again at dusk off Stepping Stones. Peanut bunker have been thick along the bridge riprap, and when the blues find them it's a five-minute free-for-all. Metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters, anything silver you can chuck fast — will get bit the second it hits the water. Bring wire leader or you'll lose half your tackle box to the first pass.

Weakfish have shown up sporadically in Manhasset Bay and up into Little Neck Bay on the early morning outgoing, mostly smaller fish mixed in with the fluke crowd, nothing to build a trip around yet but worth a few casts of a bucktail-and-bait combo if you're already out there.

Looking ahead: we're running into the first quarter moon on the 21st, which means the tidal swings are easing up through the weekend. That's actually good news for the rip fishing — Stepping Stones and the Exec Rocks current line fish better on that softer water because these bass, still working around the thermal squeeze, don't want to burn energy fighting a hard rip. Slow it down, fish the last hour of any tide change, and give the fish time to commit. I'd also keep an ear out for the first bonito scouts pushing into the Sound over the next week or two — that's usually a late-July story out here, and with warm water already stacked up from the city end to Matinecock, conditions are lining up right for it. Nothing confirmed on my end yet, but it's exactly the kind of summer that produces an early one. If I had one trip to make this week, I'd take the night bite at Execution Rocks on the bottom of the outgoing, live bunker if you can net them, and I'd have a fluke rod rigged and ready for when the sun comes up.
